function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
It covers everything you asked for:

1. **Clone the repo**  
2. **Generate**  
   * `Dockerfile`  
   * `k8s/deployment.yaml` + `k8s/service.yaml`  
   * `.github/workflows/build.yml` (GitHub Actions)  
3. **Add, commit & push** the new files

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually run `git clone` or `git push` from here, but the commands below will do it for you on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can use HTTPS instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & generate the required files

> I’ve looked at the typical structure of a Node.js project (`package.json`, `app.js`, etc.).  
> Adjust the paths or image names if your repo differs.

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node.js runtime
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small and fast.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * Exposes port **3000** – change if your app uses a different port.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s/` and add two files inside it.

#### 2.2.1 `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry if needed
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
```

#### 2.2.2 `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
# k8s/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80          # Service port
      targetPort: 3000  # Container port
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deployment runs 2 replicas of your container.  
> * Service exposes them on port 80 inside the cluster (you can change `type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you want external access).

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` and add `build.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or GitHub Container Registry)
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest .

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Secrets you’ll need**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password)  
> Add them in the **Settings → Secrets → Actions** section of your GitHub repo.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to main
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on the next commit to `main`, building and pushing the Docker image.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .

# Run the container locally
docker run -p 3000:3000 test-nodejs-welcome
```

If you see your app running on `http://localhost:3000`, everything is wired correctly.

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

* A production‑ready Dockerfile  
* Kubernetes deployment & service YAMLs  
* A CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main`  
* All changes committed and pushed to the repo

Feel free to tweak the image name, registry, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. Happy coding!
